Congruent matching profile segments (CMPS) of two bullet signatures

Source: R/cmpsc.R
cmpsc.Rd

How many pieces of one land engraved area's signature line up, at one common shift, with another's: the CMPS score of Chen et al. (2019), the count of congruent matching profile segments, with its share of the segments. A high score points to the same barrel, a low one to different barrels; no threshold is implied, since the scores of same- and different-source pairs depend on the data and the settings (Ju and Hofmann 2022).

Usage

cmpsc(a, b, len = 50, npeaks = c(5, 3, 1), tx = 25, full = FALSE)

Arguments

a

The comparison signature: numbers, NA for a missing point.

b

The reference signature, the same way.

len

The length of a basis segment in points: one whole number from 2, at most the points of a from its first value to its last.

npeaks

The number of peaks at each segment length: one to eight whole numbers from 1 (c(5, 3, 1), Chen et al.'s choice).

tx

The tolerance in points: one whole number from 0.

full

FALSE for the overlaps of cmpsR; TRUE for lags that keep a widened segment wholly inside b.

Value

An object of class cmpsc, a list: score, the number of congruent matching profile segments; nseg, the number of basis segments (the highest score possible); scaled, score / nseg; pos, the congruent lag (b[t + pos] lines up with a[t]; NA when no segment has a candidate); and segs, a data frame with one row per basis segment: seg, start (its first point in a), ccp (its candidate lag nearest pos, NA for none) and cmps.

Details

The comparison signature a, from its first value to its last, is cut into consecutive basis segments of len points (a shorter remainder at the end is dropped). Each segment is taken at the lengths len, 2 len, 4 len, ... (one per element of npeaks), widened about its centre and cut at the ends of a. At each length its cross-correlation with the reference b (Pearson correlation over the pairs with neither value missing) is computed at every lag that leaves enough pairs in common: the smaller of 0.9 times the segment's values and a tenth of the values of b, rounded, so a segment may hang over the end of b. The lags of its npeaks highest local maxima are its peaks there. A segment's candidates are the peaks of its longest length that lie within tx points of a peak at every shorter length (with one element of npeaks, all its peaks). The congruent lag is, of all the candidates in ascending order with repeats kept, the middle one (rounded up) of those that the most segments have a candidate within tx of; those segments are the congruent matching profile segments, and their number is the score. These are the rules of cmpsR (Ju and Hofmann 2022), which cmpsc() reproduces exactly, including a lag that falls on a half point when the overlap needed is not a whole number of points.

With full = TRUE a lag is used only when the widened segment lies wholly inside b: correlations from a few points at the ends are left out, at the price of segments near the ends that cannot reach their lag (and a reference shorter than a widened segment gives no peaks, where the default refuses it). The scores then differ from cmpsR's by about one segment on simulated pairs.

Signatures are taken as they come (detrended profiles, as bulletxtrctr extracts them; Hare et al. 2017), in points of one spacing; chmb() compares the raw profiles of tool marks instead.

References

Chen, Z., Chu, W., Soons, J. A., Thompson, R. M., Song, J. and Zhao, X. (2019). Fired bullet signature correlation using the Congruent Matching Profile Segments (CMPS) method. Forensic Science International, 305, 109964. doi:10.1016/j.forsciint.2019.109964

Ju, W. and Hofmann, H. (2022). An open-source implementation of the CMPS algorithm for assessing similarity of bullets. The R Journal, 14(2), 268-287. doi:10.32614/RJ-2022-035

Hare, E., Hofmann, H. and Carriquiry, A. (2017). Automatic matching of bullet land impressions. The Annals of Applied Statistics, 11(4), 2332-2356. doi:10.1214/17-AOAS1080

Examples

set.seed(1)
a <- cumsum(rnorm(600, sd = 0.5)) + sin(seq_len(600) / 9)
b <- a[31:600] + rnorm(570, sd = 0.1)
cmpsc(a, b)
#> cmpsc: 11 of 12 segments congruent (0.9166667) at lag -30
cmpsc(a, cumsum(rnorm(570, sd = 0.5)))$score
#> [1] 2
